input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.

Topic: CSCI-620: Introduction to Big Data. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course provides a broad introduction to the exploration and management of large datasets being generated and used in the modern world. First, practical techniques used in exploratory data analysis and mining are introduced; topics include data preparation, visualization, statistics for understanding data, and grouping and prediction techniques. Second, approaches used to store, retrieve, and manage data in the real world are presented; topics include traditional database systems, query languages, and data integrity and quality. Case studies will examine issues in data capture, organization, storage, retrieval, visualization, and analysis in diverse settings such as urban crime, drug research, census data, social networking, and space exploration. Big data exploration and management projects, a term paper and a presentation are required. Sufficient background in database systems and statistics is recommended. Prereq: (CSCI-603 or CSCI-605 with a grade of B or better) or (CSCI-320 or SWEN-344). May not take & receive credit for CSCI-620 & CSCI-420/420H. If earned credit for/or currently enrolled in CSCI-420/420H you will not be permitted to enroll in CSCI-620. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer Regeneration revision 2: use ten distinct, specific beat titles and avoid repeating any title or section label. The previous draft failed local validation. CSCI-620: repeated beat title detected Return only the requested structured lesson blueprint. Produce ten distinct beats with complete claims, examples, and visual directions. Every claim must be directly supported by its cited excerpt and reuse important technical terms from that source. Do not discuss these instructions or include schema examples in any field.

Source excerpts:

[postgresql-documentation]
Data systems organize records with declared types, tables, rows, columns, keys, and constraints. Queries select, join, aggregate, order, and transform data. Indexes provide additional access paths for selected workloads. Transactions group operations and isolation controls how concurrent operations observe one another. Query planning and physical storage affect performance without changing logical query meaning. Analytical work should preserve provenance from captured data through cleaning, transformation, grouping, modeling, visualization, and reporting. Data quality analysis makes missingness, duplicates, inconsistent representation, integrity constraints, sampling, and update behavior explicit.

[rit-csci-620]
This course provides a broad introduction to the exploration and management of large datasets being generated and used in the modern world. First, practical techniques used in exploratory data analysis and mining are introduced; topics include data preparation, visualization, statistics for understanding data, and grouping and prediction techniques. Second, approaches used to store, retrieve, and manage data in the real world are presented; topics include traditional database systems, query languages, and data integrity and quality. Case studies will examine issues in data capture, organization, storage, retrieval, visualization, and analysis in diverse settings such as urban crime, drug research, census data, social networking, and space exploration. Big data exploration and management projects, a term paper and a presentation are required. Sufficient background in database systems and statistics is recommended. Prereq: (CSCI-603 or CSCI-605 with a grade of B or better) or (CSCI-320 or SWEN-344). May not take & receive credit for CSCI-620 & CSCI-420/420H. If earned credit for/or currently enrolled in CSCI-420/420H you will not be permitted to enroll in CSCI-620. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

[scikit-learn-user-guide]
Data-analysis workflows separate data preparation, exploratory analysis, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation. Supervised methods learn mappings from examples paired with target labels, while unsupervised methods identify structure without targets. Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage. Pipelines combine transformations and estimators so the same operations are applied consistently. Cross-validation repeats training and validation across defined splits. Grouping, dimensionality reduction, classification, regression, and clustering answer different questions and require appropriate assumptions and metrics. Evaluation must match the task and the cost of errors, while distribution shift, missing data, overfitting, and unexamined sampling choices can invalidate conclusions.

beats.claim: Big data exploration and management focuses on the exploration and management of large datasets being generated and used in the modern world.
beats.example: Urban crime datasets require systematic exploration to identify patterns in location, frequency, and temporal trends.
beats.title: Foundations of Big Data Exploration
beats.visualDirection: Display a map overlay showing urban crime hotspots with a legend explaining data density and temporal filters.

beats.claim: Data-analysis workflows separate data preparation, exploratory analysis, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation.
beats.example: Cleaning census data involves handling missing values and standardizing categorical variables before analysis.
beats.title: Data Preparation and Workflow Structure
beats.visualDirection: Show a linear workflow diagram with nodes for preparation, exploration, training, validation, and evaluation, connected by directional arrows.

beats.claim: Supervised methods learn mappings from examples paired with target labels, while unsupervised methods identify structure without targets.
beats.example: Predicting drug response requires supervised learning with patient outcomes as labels, whereas clustering patient demographics uses unsupervised methods.
beats.title: Supervised and Unsupervised Learning Methods
beats.visualDirection: Split a diagram into two columns: left shows labeled examples mapping to outcomes, right shows unlabeled data forming clusters.

beats.claim: Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage.
beats.example: Scaling features using only the training set mean and standard deviation prevents test set information from influencing model parameters.
beats.title: Preprocessing and Data Leakage Prevention
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a pipeline where a scaler transforms training data, then applies the same transformation to validation data without recalculating parameters.

beats.claim: Pipelines combine transformations and estimators so the same operations are applied consistently.
beats.example: A machine learning pipeline applies standardization, imputation, and feature selection sequentially to ensure reproducible results.
beats.title: Pipelines and Consistent Transformations
beats.visualDirection: Render a horizontal pipeline graphic with icons for each step, showing data flowing through and emerging as a final model output.

beats.claim: Cross-validation repeats training and validation across defined splits, and evaluation must match the task and the cost of errors.
beats.example: K-fold cross-validation evaluates a classification model for social networking fraud detection by rotating validation sets across training folds.
beats.title: Cross-Validation and Model Evaluation
beats.visualDirection: Draw a circular diagram with five segments labeled as folds, highlighting one fold as validation while others are training, with a metric box showing accuracy.

beats.claim: Traditional database systems organize records with declared types, tables, rows, columns, keys, and constraints.
beats.example: A hospital database stores patient records in tables with defined data types, primary keys, and foreign key constraints to maintain referential integrity.
beats.title: Traditional Database Systems and Query Languages
beats.visualDirection: Show a relational schema diagram with tables, columns, data types, primary keys, and foreign key relationships between them.

beats.claim: Queries select, join, aggregate, order, and transform data, while indexes provide additional access paths for selected workloads.
beats.example: A query joins patient records with medication logs, aggregates daily prescriptions, orders by date, and uses an index on the date column to speed up retrieval.
beats.title: Query Operations and Indexing
beats.visualDirection: Display a SQL query structure with highlighted SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY, ORDER BY clauses, alongside an index tree diagram showing optimized data access.

beats.claim: Data quality analysis makes missingness, duplicates, inconsistent representation, integrity constraints, sampling, and update behavior explicit.
beats.example: A census dataset requires explicit handling of duplicate household records, inconsistent address formats, and missing population counts before analysis.
beats.title: Data Quality and Integrity Management
beats.visualDirection: Present a checklist graphic listing missingness, duplicates, inconsistent representation, integrity constraints, sampling, and update behavior as quality metrics.

beats.claim: Analytical work should preserve provenance from captured data through cleaning, transformation, grouping, modeling, visualization, and reporting.
beats.example: A space exploration project maintains a traceable log from raw satellite telemetry through cleaning, transformation, grouping, modeling, visualization, and final reporting.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Show a circular provenance loop with arrows connecting each stage: captured data, cleaning, transformation, grouping, modeling, visualization, reporting, and back to captured data.

2. Explain the architectural and operational principles of traditional database systems, query languages, and data integrity mechanisms.
3. Apply practical problem-solving methods to analyze data quality, manage missingness, and evaluate model performance using appropriate metrics.

Consider this worked case: A query joins patient records with medication logs, aggregates daily prescriptions, orders by date, and uses an index on the date column to speed up retrieval. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.

Data systems organize records with declared types, tables, rows, columns, keys, and constraints. Consider this worked case: A hospital database stores patient records in tables with defined data types, primary keys, and foreign key constraints to maintain referential integrity. Supervised methods learn mappings from examples paired with target labels, while unsupervised methods identify structure without targets.
